subtopic: Facing peer pressure to do something unsafe
subtype: Approach: leaving the situation and telling a trusted adult [Action]
passage:
Dear Preeti,

I know you're angry that I left on Saturday. Here is what happened for me. When the others began planning to climb the old quarry wall at night and dared each of us, I said no twice and they kept going. My stomach was tight. I told them I was leaving, walked out and rang my uncle from the road, and he came in ten minutes. On Monday I went to see the school counsellor and explained the plan, because if I said nothing, someone might get hurt. The counsellor listened, thanked me, and said they would speak with the adults. I miss the fun of the group. But I would rather have you angry than have anyone hurt. If you want to talk, I'll be at the library on Thursday.

Ritu

qa.q: Who did Ritu ring from the road?
qa.a: Ritu rang an uncle, who came in ten minutes.

qa.q: How does Ritu feel about leaving and telling the counsellor?
qa.a: Ritu feels torn: Ritu misses the group's fun and expects Preeti's anger, but stays firm about safety, with a tight stomach at the time.

qa.q: What else could Ritu do to help Preeti understand, and why?
qa.a: Ritu could ask Preeti to come along to the counsellor or talk it over with a parent, because hearing it from a trusted adult may make the danger more real.

qa.q: How might Preeti see Ritu's leaving?
qa.a: Preeti may feel angry and let down, taking it as disloyalty, though the letter shows Ritu cared enough to keep everyone safe.

grounding: When pressure continues, the student walks out, calls a parent or uncle, and later tells the school counsellor about the dangerous plan, putting safety above group loyalty.

subtopic: Facing peer pressure to do something unsafe
subtype: Approach: leaving the situation and telling a trusted adult [Action]
passage: Hafsa, you asked why Vivek's gang stopped talking to me. Everyone's calling me Jomon the snitch now, so let me tell it properly. Saturday night I was at Vivek's with five others. His parents were away, and around nine they started planning to take his father's car to the beach. Vivek's fifteen. He's never driven on a main road. When I said no, they called me a coward and kept pushing. So I walked out, stood at the gate and called my uncle. He came in ten minutes, took me home, and phoned Vivek's father on the way. They didn't go that night, but on Sunday they were planning it for next weekend. So on Monday I told the counsellor. She called Vivek's parents that same afternoon. They're angry at me. I'd still rather that than someone getting hurt.

qa.q: Who did Jomon call from the gate?
How does Jomon feel about being called a snitch?
qa.a: Jomon is hurt by it but steady, preferring the friends' anger to someone getting hurt.

qa.q: Why was telling the counsellor important even after that night?
qa.a: The group was planning it again for the next weekend, so an adult who could reach the parents had to know.

qa.q: How might Vivek's parents feel after the counsellor's call?
qa.a: They are likely shocked and worried to hear of the plan, and glad to know in time to stop it.

grounding: A student tells of walking out when pressure continued, calling an uncle and later telling the counsellor about a dangerous driving plan.

passage: I was there when Mohit walked out, so I know it wasn't easy. After school on Friday a bunch of us were at the old railway bridge, and Sahil said the plan was to stand on the ledge and film the express going past, close enough to feel the wind. The others were cheering. Mohit said, "Guys, that's actually how people die." They laughed and called him chicken. He said it again. They laughed louder. So he picked up his bag, walked to the road, and I saw him on the phone, pacing. Twenty minutes later his mother's scooter pulled up, and she marched straight to the bridge and sent everyone home. On Monday Mohit went to Uma Ma'am, the counsellor, and by lunch she had spoken to our whole class. I don't know how he felt walking away. He didn't look back.

qa.q: What did Sahil plan to film?
qa.a: The express going past, from the ledge, close enough to feel the wind.

qa.q: What might Mohit have felt as he repeated his warning and was laughed at?
qa.a: He likely felt angry and anxious, frustrated that they wouldn't listen but worried enough to keep trying.
He didn't argue endlessly; he left, called his mother, who came and sent everyone home, and then told the counsellor so the whole class was spoken to.

qa.q: How did the narrator see Mohit walking away?
qa.a: The narrator saw it wasn't easy, watched him pace on the phone, and couldn't tell how he felt, only that he didn't look back.

grounding: An observer describes a student leaving a dangerous railway plan, calling a parent and telling the counsellor, putting safety over group loyalty.
